Where plunder is forbidden (the Crimea's provost, the Lieber Code of 1863, the Hague rules of 1907), or past what a man may keep as a trophy, the provost rolls his Watch against the man's Stealth: if the provost wins, the loot is taken from him, and on the provost's critical or the man's fumble the era's punishment follows (hanging, flogging, a court-martial). In the eras of prize money each man draws his rank's shares (at Waterloo, a private one share of about 51 days' pay, a captain 35). A medieval or Thirty Years' War prisoner may be ransomed (with leave).

Honours. The Plains nations had no ranks and no pay. A man's honours come from coups counted (the first to strike counts most: the roller counts it when his blow lands in close combat) and horses taken from an enemy camp; his horses are his wealth, and giving them away turns wealth into standing.

Sickness

Before antibiotics, disease emptied armies faster than battle. Once a week every well man may catch what the camp breeds, at a chance set by its hygiene (a bivouac is poor, quarters good, other camps fair), by staying long in one place, by the ground and by the weather. A case climbs to its peak and then gets better or worse on the track of Recovery. The sick cannot march on their own, and a force carrying them on litters is slowed. Scurvy comes after weeks without fresh food, frostbite on the coldest nights. The diseases, the costs, scurvy and frostbite are in Sickness in full.

The retinue: on the road

The retinue marches north on foot: 20 miles (32 km) a day on the road when the days are long, less in March, when Towton was fought, and less again in the snow that fell that day. It makes a watched camp each night, with a sentry roster and fires; no tools are needed. In a fair camp, moving on every day, the flux is the only real danger; were it to sit in a filthy siege camp for a month, typhus would come for it.

For the GM

The travel map counts all of this for whole forces, and runs each named character's own case with his own Endurance when you put him With a force from the roller. Your job is the choices: how hard to march, where to camp, whether to wait for the sick.

Weather, light and works

The day's weather

Each day on the travel map rolls its weather from the climate's figures for the month: its highs and lows, its days of rain and fog, its winds. Wet and dry spells last, and a warm or cold spell carries over. Rain falls as snow when the day's high is 36 °F (2 °C) or less. The GM can roll again or set any of it by hand. A sandstorm is never rolled: a battlefield names it (73 Easting, 1991) or the GM sets it.

Mud and snow build up and wear off day by day. On the travel map they slow the going; on the battle map, mud or snow at level 2 or more costs one more hex of movement every hex. Heavy rain or a storm floods the fords for 2 days, counting that day.

Weather in a fight

Weather affects missiles, never close combat:

Weather Can aim to Bows and crossbows
Fair no limit —
Overcast no limit —
Fog 55 yards (50 m) —
Rain 328 yards (300 m) −10%
Heavy rain 164 yards (150 m) −20%
Storm 109 yards (100 m) −20%
Snow 164 yards (150 m) −10%
Heavy snow 87 yards (80 m) −10%
Blizzard 33 yards (30 m) −20%
Sandstorm 437 yards (400 m) —
Wind Bows, slings, thrown Firearms Range bands with or into it
Calm or light air — — —
Breeze — — ±10%
Strong wind −10% — ±20%
Gale −20% −10% ±30%

Shooting with the wind lengthens the range bands of bows, crossbows, slings and thrown weapons; shooting into it shortens them, and rain or snow in a shooter's face halves how far he can see to aim. Into a strong wind they also lose 10%, into a gale 20%. In the wet, a muzzle-loader can misfire, losing the shot (Misfires, in Black-powder guns).

Cold. In hard frost (5 °F, -15 °C, or colder) machine guns, submachine guns and assault rifles misfire 10% more, as oil thickens and actions freeze; in bitter cold (-13 °F, -25 °C) 25% more, and every hex costs 1 more to cross. A battle sent from the travel map takes its cold from the day's low.

Fatigue

A hard march, heat or cold, deep going, a bad night and hand-to-hand fighting tire a character a step at a time; a good night's rest takes it back. On the field map whole units tire the same way, from hand-to-hand fighting and deep going (an exchange):

Fatigue Attack and defence Marching speed
Fresh — 100%
Tired −5% 100%
Weary −10% 90%
Exhausted −20% 75%
Spent −30% 0%

Light and the dark

In the dark no one can see to aim, or to call fire, past the light's reach, and aimed fire is harder: on a moonlit night 109 yards (100 m), on a dark night 55 yards (50 m). The weather's own limit still applies, and whichever is shorter counts. A battlefield can change the light as its battle goes on, at sunset or dawn. Night-vision devices of the later wars see further (Night vision, in Air and night devices):

Light Can see to aim Aimed fire
Daylight no limit —
Dusk or dawn 219 yards (200 m) −5%
Moonlit night 109 yards (100 m) −10%
Dark night 55 yards (50 m) −20%

The dark also slows a march and turns men round:

Light Movement Losing direction
Daylight — —
Dusk or dawn — —
Moonlit night +1 a hex 10%
Dark night +1 a hex 25%
  • Losing direction. Each unit that moved in the dark may lose its way when its side's move ends. Its chance is the light's, adjusted by its quality: green +12%, regular +5%, veteran −3%. A lost unit ends a point off its line, a hex astray that way (unless that is blocked or touches the enemy), and cannot move next exchange, though it can turn.
  • Muzzle flashes. A unit that fires when the light limits sight to less than 328 yards (300 m) shows where it is. Through the next exchange, the hexes it fired from can be aimed at, and fire called on, from up to 328 yards (300 m) away.
  • Flares. A flare lights the ground within 109 yards (100 m) for 2 exchanges, and illumination rounds from mortars and guns light far more. A lit hex is seen as by day.
  • The enemy commander knows only what its units see, so at night it waits for the enemy to come close or to fire.

For the GM

Night evens the odds against a stronger side, and its fire support and aircraft count for less in the dark. A defender with fixed lines, flares and a plan for illumination can still hold.

Works

Camps and battlefields have works: along a hex's sides (ditches, banks, palisades, gates, walls) or in a hex (stakes, felled trees, wagons, trenches, bunkers):

Work Cover Crossing Blocks close combat
Ditch — +2 movement —
Earth bank −20% +1 movement —
Palisade −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) yes
Gate −40% free yes
Stone wall −50% cannot be crossed (ladders; from 1914, charges or heavy shells) yes
Stakes — +1 movement —
Abatis −20% +2 movement —
Pavise −20% free —
Wagon −40% cannot be crossed (breach it) —
Barbed wire — +3 movement —
Bunker −50% +1 movement —
Trench −40% +1 movement —
Downed helicopter −30% +2 movement —

A palisade, barred gate or wagon must be breached to get through: men hack at it instead of fighting, until it is down. No axe opens a stone wall. On the field map, once the armies carry demolition charges (from 1914), men ordered to breach blow a gap in it, and a shell or bomb bursting beside it opens it at the firing kind's knock-out chance, as it knocks out a bunker (heavy howitzers, tanks and aircraft; not mortars or field guns). Before that, men go over it only with ladders. Across a palisade, wall or barred gate only reach-2 weapons strike, from the front rank, and striking up a bank or ditch costs its height. Mounted men cannot enter stakes, felled trees, wagons, wire, trenches, bunkers or wrecks.

On the field map, men on foot the GM marks with ladders can escalade a palisade, wall or barred gate instead: a few men a hex fight from the ladders at −20%, the defenders strike back at them, and once the far side is clear the unit can climb over at a cost of 4 hexes of movement.

For the GM

Weather is the cheapest way to change a fight. Rain on the morning of a battle takes the archers' edge away and spoils matchlocks; fog lets the attackers close unseen; a gale at the archers' backs carries their arrows nearly a third further. Roll it, then let the players decide whether to fight in it.

Other wars

Everything so far has used the medieval tables. The same rules carry a team through 10 more eras, from the Thirty Years' War to Afghanistan. Each era has its own skills, origins, careers, events, armies, teams, followers and jobs. Pick one with Era in the team builder.

Each period has its own book with its armies' figures, the wound tables its battles roll on and its battlefields: The Medieval Wars (c.1180–1500), The Black-Powder Wars (1618–1877), The World Wars (1914–1945), Korea and Vietnam (1950–1973), The Late Wars (1982–2014).

The eras

Era Armies Fighting skills Careers A term
Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) The Swedish army (Swedes, Finns, Scots and Germans), The Imperial army and the Catholic League Musket, Pistol, Blade, Pike 10 4 years
Horse and musket (1775-1815) The Continental Army (1775-1783), The British Army in America (1775-1783), The British in the Peninsula (1808-1814), The French Empire in Spain (1808-1814), The United States (1812-1815) Musket, Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 12 4 years
Crimean War (1854-1856) British, French, Russian Musket, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 11 4 years
Plains nations (1860-1877) The Lakota (Oglala, Minneconjou and other bands), The Cheyenne and Arapaho Bow, Lance, Club and knife, Gun 7 4 years
Civil War and frontier (1861-1876) The Union (1861-1865), The Confederacy (1861-1865), The US Army on the frontier (1866-1876) Rifle, Pistol, Blade, Bayonet, Gunnery 11 4 years
First World War (1914-1918) The British Empire, Newfoundland, France, Germany, The United States (1917-1918), Russian, Serbian, Austro-Hungarian, Bulgarian Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Bombing, Gunnery, Bayonet, Trench weapons 12 1 year
Second World War (1939-1945) The United States in Europe, US Marines and Army in the Pacific, The British Commonwealth, Germany, Italian, The Soviet Union, Japan Rifle, SMG and pistol, Machine gun, Grenade, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 13 1 year

The Falklands to Afghanistan (1982-2014) UK 1982, Argentina 1982, US 1991, US 1993, Russia 1995, Chechens, US 2003-14, UK 2003-14, Insurgents, Iraq 2003, Peshmerga 2003 Rifle, Pistol, Machine gun, Grenade and rocket, Gunnery, Bayonet, Close combat 12 1 year

Brawl, Parry and Dodge carry over to every era, and so do the skills used outside a fight (Leechcraft, Fieldcraft, Watch, Stealth and the rest). Bow, Crossbow, Axe and mace, Polearm and Sling stay medieval (the Plains nations have their own Bow). Gunnery is the skill of men who serve guns and mortars (and, in the Crimea, of sailors serving ships' guns ashore), rocket launchers and recoilless rifles in Korea, recoilless rifles in Vietnam, and guided missiles in the late wars. In the Crimea one Musket skill covers both the smoothbore musket and the rifle-musket. From Vietnam on, the RPG is fired with Grenade and rocket.

What changes

  • A term. Before 1914 a career term is 4 years, as in the medieval tables. From the First World War on, a term is 1 year of the war, so a soldier of three terms is about twenty-one.
  • Wound tables. Each army rolls on its own war's wound table, both for old wounds when a character is made and in the roller. Where a war's records have no wounds of some kind, the table borrows the nearest one: the pike's thrusts are rolled on the Visby melee table, and the frontier's gunshots come from the Civil War table.

  • Armour. It follows the army and the year:

    • pikemen's and cuirassiers' armours in the 1630s;
    • the steel helmet from 1915–16;
    • nylon flak vests in Korea and Vietnam;
    • plate armour in Iraq and Afghanistan.

    Many armies wore none. A vest's rating against each threat (fragments, pistol rounds, rifle rounds) decides how many steps it takes off a wound, so a vest that stops a grenade fragment may do nothing against a rifle bullet. The roller and the field map read the same kits.

  • Kit and weapons come with the career and the army: a Viet Cong RPG gunner carries an RPG, a Second World War tank crewman a submachine gun.

  • Names are common names of the period and place, put together at random, and are not meant to name anyone. Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese names are written family name first.

Women under arms

Where the records show women serving in a career, the team builder can roll a woman for it at that army's share. A career with its own share (in brackets below) rolls at that instead: the camp women of the Thirty Years' War's baggage train, the French vivandières (four to a battalion from 1793), the British soldiers' wives on the strength (six in a hundred men went overseas, by lot), the nurses from Scutari to Vietnam, the auxiliaries of both world wars (the ATS made up two-thirds of the crews of Britain's mixed heavy anti-aircraft batteries), and the Female Engagement Teams of Iraq and Afghanistan. Women who fought are open where the records show them, chosen rather than rolled: the townswomen who defended Toulouse in 1218 and Dunbar in 1338, Margaret Corbin at her husband's gun and Deborah Sampson in the Continental line, the Lakota and Cheyenne women at the Rosebud and the Little Bighorn, the Russian women's battalions of 1917 (Bochkareva's reached the third German line at Smorgon), Serbia's women sergeants and Flora Sandes, a British nurse who enlisted as a private in the retreat of 1915, Austria-Hungary's few (Viktoria Savs, disguised as a man with the Standschützen; Olena Stepaniv, an officer of the Ukrainian Sich Riflemen), the North Vietnamese and Viet Cong women who fought, guided and cleared bombs on the Trail, and the South Vietnamese army's women medics. In every other army a career rolls a man, and the page gives the reason. An army's share is the women among its soldiers as a whole, not just in that career, so treat it as a rough guide. A GM may prefer to choose.

Women under arms: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Deborah Sampson, 1782-1783

On 20 May 1782 Deborah Sampson, aged 21, enlisted at Uxbridge, Massachusetts, as "Robert Shurtleff", in the light infantry company of the 4th Massachusetts Regiment. In a skirmish near Tarrytown, New York, that summer she took a cut to the forehead and a musket ball in the thigh. She let a surgeon dress her head and left before he could see to the leg. Her own later accounts say she dug one ball out with a penknife and a needle, and that a second stayed in her for life; no one else saw it. In the summer of 1783 she fell ill with fever in Philadelphia, and the doctor who treated her found her out. She was honourably discharged at West Point in October 1783 (the 23rd or the 25th: sources differ). Massachusetts paid her withheld wages in 1792, and from 1805 Congress paid her an invalid's pension of $4 a month. Her later claim to have fought at Yorktown is false: she enlisted after it.

For the GM

Pick an era for the fighting you want, not the uniforms. Before the machine gun, battles are decided in the press and the rout, as in the medieval chapters. From 1914 on, men are put down by fire they never see, and what matters is cover, going to ground and the guns. The next chapters cover that.

Money by era

A Day is a common soldier's day's pay in his army's coin: the rules count in Days so that a price in 1415 and one in 2008 can be weighed against each other, but every price was set down in the money of its time, and the pages show that money first, with the Days after it. Where a coin has no soldier's pay to measure it by, its prices stand in the coin alone.

The Day in each army's coin

The Day in each army's coin: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Playing alone

Grave Wounds can be played by one person. The pages take the GM's work that needs no judgement: the enemy's moves on the field map, its blows on the roller, the march, the weather, sickness and the camp. What is left is the judgement, and for that you ask the dice.

How a session runs

  1. Make a team in the team builder and send it to the roller, as in Making a team. Pick a battlefield from a period book, or a campaign map on the travel map.
  2. Open the campaign page. It follows the pages through muster, march, fight, aftermath and downtime, and keeps the game's log and save.
  3. March on the travel map. Its clock stops when your force meets the enemy. Ask the dice anything the map does not say: is the farm empty, will the villagers sell bread.
  4. Fight. A skirmish goes to the roller: turn on Run the fight, play your own men, and let the GM's script play the other side; Play to my turn runs it until it is yours. A battle goes to the field map: give the other side to the enemy commander, attacking or holding as the battlefield says, and move your own units. Your team fights among them as heroes.
  5. After the fight, bind the wounded, carry them to camp and roll their recovery, as in Recovery. On the roller, Send the result to the travel map takes the fight's dead, wounded and prisoners back to the forces, and the beaten one falls back; then rest in camp (Rest until tomorrow on the campaign page) while the wounds mend. This is where a solo campaign is won or lost.
  6. Compare your battle with the one fought, and with the enemy commander. On the field map a battlefield laid out with its armies as drawn up shows Beat history: how the battle went, how often the commander wins each side playing against itself, and, when the battle has ended by itself, your result against both. You beat the commander with a better outcome than its median run, or the same outcome at a better rate of their men lost for each of yours. Each battlefield's section in its period book tells how it really went, and what it cost.

Playing it straight

Alone, you are the GM as well as the players, so be a fair one. Ask the dice before you look at what the answer would cost you, and take the answer the dice give. Let the commander have the enemy's choices, not you.

Ask the dice

When a question has no rule and no page to answer it, put it as a yes-or-no question, decide how likely a yes is, and roll d100 as for any test:

How likely Roll at or under
Almost certain 90
Likely 70
Even 50
Unlikely 30
Hardly possible 10
  • At or under: yes. A critical (10% of the chance or under) is yes, and more than you asked for.
  • Over: no. A fumble (96 or more) is no, and worse than you feared.
  • Within 5 either side of the number: the answer comes with a complication. Roll d10:
d10 Complication
1 Someone saw: an enemy, a villager or a rival now knows where you are
2 It costs time: half a day, or an exchange on the field
3 It costs something: food, ammunition, a horse, a day's pay
4 A man is hurt doing it: a fall, a kick, a cut (a light wound on the roller)
5 Someone wants something in return
6 The weather turns: roll the day's weather again, worse
7 It splits the team: one man is somewhere else for a day
8 An old trouble comes back: a debt, a grudge, a wound that opens
9 A stranger joins you, not entirely welcome
10 The enemy is nearer than you thought

Ask only what matters, and let the answer stand. Two questions about the same thing are one question asked twice.

The retinue: the barn

On the road to Towton the retinue needs shelter for a wet night. Is the barn ahead empty? It is Lancastrian country, so Unlikely: 30. The roll is 33, within 5 of the number: no, with a complication. The d10 gives 1: men are sleeping in the barn, and one of them has seen the retinue's fire.

Modules

The core rules are written for blades, bows and armour, and they hold for every period. A module adds what a period's weapons bring onto the field. Each period book says which modules it switches on; leave the others out.

Module What it brings Switched on by
Black-powder guns Batteries, canister and round shot; misfires in the wet; storming works with the bayonet The Black-Powder Wars
Modern fire Extended order, rifles, machine guns, going to ground, digging in; fire support and barrages; trenches and bunkers; fixed lines; more men put down The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam and The Late Wars; The Black-Powder Wars for its breech-loaders only
Armour and mines Tanks, carriers and lorries; anti-tank guns; minefields and sappers; riders The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam and The Late Wars
Air and night devices Night vision; aircraft and air controllers; landing by air The World Wars for aircraft from 1944; Korea and Vietnam and The Late Wars

Black-powder guns

For the wars from the Thirty Years' War to the 1870s: guns that fire round shot, canister and shell, muzzle-loaders that fail in the wet, and infantry that carry works with the bayonet.

Guns of the black-powder wars

A battery is a unit in battery order, 20 men to a hex, its crews 10 to a gun: as crews fall, fewer guns are served. Each served gun fires a round an exchange at the nearest enemy in sight, out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m) (1,750 yards (1,600 m) rifled): canister within 328 yards (300 m), round shot beyond (which ploughs through a deep column and bounds on over firm ground), and shell from howitzers, over anything in the way. Each gun carries 50 rounds; limbering or unlimbering takes an exchange; a battery that breaks loses its guns. Charged in front, it fires one round of canister before the melee. The shot in full is in Batteries in full.

Misfires

In the wet, a muzzle-loader can misfire, losing the shot. The chance depends on how it fires its charge: a slow match, a wheel-lock, a flint, or a percussion cap. A breech-loader's cartridge does not misfire in the rain.

Ignition Rain or snow Heavy rain, storm, blizzard
Match 30% 60%
Wheel 15% 30%
Flint 15% 30%
Percussion 5% 10%
Cartridge — —

Storming works

Attacking, infantry with muskets, rifle-muskets or breech-loaders do not stop to trade fire with an enemy behind works (a parapet, trench or bank), dug in, or in buildings or rubble. They close without seeking cover, firing as they go, and charge it, with the same odds. Flintlock riflemen, archers and machine guns still fight by fire. A wall or palisade that blocks hand-to-hand fighting stops them at its foot, unless they carry ladders: then they go up it (see works). Breaching it is the GM's order.

Modern fire

For the wars of machine guns, quick-firing artillery and breech-loaders. The field map uses the same exchange for every era; what this module changes is the weight of fire, and how men live under it. A period book may switch on only part of it, as the black-powder book does for its breech-loaders.

Modern infantry

  • Extended order. 3 men to a hex, a few yards apart. Shots at them count half, and they move 8 hexes.
  • Rifles. In a minute a bolt-action rifle fires 10 rounds, a self-loading or assault rifle 15, and a submachine gun or pistol 12. They are rolled as aimed shots at the same rate as a musket's: most rounds are fired at the enemy's line, not at a man.
  • Modern fire puts men down. Against breech-loaders and later weapons, shell and grenades, every serious or critical wound puts a man down, and a light one calls for the stop check (An exchange): the casualty returns from 1914 on count nearly every man hit as out of the line.
  • Storming in bounds. Attacking, modern rifles and sub-machine guns storm works as black-powder infantry do (Storming works), but in bounds: a unit fired on in the last exchange (whether or not anyone fell) goes to ground and fires this move, and goes on once a bound draws no fire, its target is pinned, or it can charge home. From the Second World War on, every advance goes this way, not only against works.
  • Going to ground. On its own move a unit can go to ground in the folds of the ground. Shots at it lose 15% on top of its cover. It cannot move until it gets up, but it still shoots and fights hand to hand.
  • Digging in. A unit with a modern weapon, out of contact, can dig shell scrapes and foxholes: 3 exchanges without moving or firing, and it is dug in where it stands. Dug in, it counts as gone to ground (and hidden, and steadier) while it stays there, but it can get up and move, leaving its holes. In set-up the GM can start units dug in.
  • Hidden men. Men gone to ground, in a trench or a bunker, or in buildings or rubble show little of themselves. Only 10% of the aimed shots at them find a man to aim at (5% of a machine gun's); the rest go at the smoke and the flashes. Dug-in men also hold better: +10 on morale.
  • Machine guns. A machine-gun team serves one gun for every 5 men, and the gun fires while one of its crew is up. It fires 300 rounds a minute, and one in 10 is rolled as an aimed shot.
  • The beaten zone. The cone of fire falls on past its target. The first other unit (friend or foe) within 219 yards (200 m) beyond the target on the line of fire takes 50% as many shots. Woods, rough ground, marsh, buildings, tall buildings and rubble stop it.
  • Pinned. A unit near a shell burst, or under a machine gun's fire (in its beaten zone too), checks at the end of the exchange: d100 against its Nerve, +10 if gone to ground. On a failure it is pinned for the next exchange: it cannot move, and it shoots at half its rate.

Fire support

From the First World War on, a side can have batteries off the map: mortars, field guns, heavy howitzers, and tanks or autocannon firing over open sights. Each is a number of tubes with their rounds and crews.

Kind Reach Shells a minute a tube Rounds a tube Lands Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes
Mortars 2.2 miles (3.6 km) 3 60 this exchange 2 hexes 15, 5, 1
Field guns 6.8 miles (11 km) 2 80 next exchange 4 hexes 20, 8, 3, 1
Heavy howitzers 9.0 miles (14.5 km) 1 40 next exchange 5 hexes 30, 12, 5, 2, 1, 0.5
Tanks (direct fire) in sight 2 60 this exchange none 25, 5
Autocannon (direct fire) in sight 3 300 this exchange none 20
  • Calling fire. On its side's move a battery fires on a hex that one of the side's units can see. That means within the weather's sight and the light's, with no woods or smoke between. It can keep firing each exchange until stopped or out of rounds.
  • Where it lands. Each shell scatters by a d6 for the direction and up to the kind's scatter in hexes.
  • What it does. Every man in the burst is struck at the % for his distance from it, ×0.35 if gone to ground and less his cover. A struck man rolls a wound as one hit by shell fragments at 70%. With quick-play, add up each man's chance (men × their % for each burst) for the average and roll once on the spread chart for the men struck.
  • Tree bursts. Over woods, shells burst in the branches. The woods give no cover, the chance is ×1.5, and going to ground only brings it to ×0.7.
  • Smoke spends the same rounds and wounds no one. No one sees or shoots into, out of or through it, and it drifts downwind:
Wind Exchanges it screens after landing Drifts (hexes an exchange)
Calm or light air 3 —
Breeze 2 1
Strong wind 1 2
Gale none: blown away 2
  • Illumination lights the ground round its aim as by day (see Light and the dark). It needs no one to see the hex.
  • A fire plan. A creeping barrage lifts its aim 1 to 3 hexes after 1 to 4 exchanges on each line, ahead of an advance kept to the same timetable. A plan can have up to eight legs, each going on the same way or turning.

  • Counter-battery. A battery that has fired is located (not tanks or autocannon firing over open sights). Field guns and heavy howitzers can fire on it with no one needing to see it:

    • each shell lands among its guns at 2% (field guns) or 4% (heavy howitzers), knocking out a tube and striking 2 of its crew;
    • at 3 times that chance, it bursts close by and strikes one man.

    Counter-battery wears a battery down over a battle rather than ending it. Displacing silences a battery for an exchange or more and leaves it no longer located.

  • On the map. A battery can stand on a hex of the map instead. From there it reaches only its range, and an enemy unit next to it overruns it.

Trenches and bunkers

A trench gives the men in it cover and hides them, but they fight hand to hand as usual. A bunker shelters its men from shots and shellfire and from blows: no one strikes them, and they strike no one, but they shoot out of it. A tank's shell bursting on it knocks it out at 8%, a heavy howitzer's at 2%.

To take a bunker, a unit next to it storms it with one of three means, once an exchange for each enemy-held bunker across its front, +20 if the bunker's men are pinned:

Means Knocks the bunker out on d100 Men in its hex struck
Grenades 10 or less 40%, as grenade wounds
Satchel charges 25 or less 60%, as grenade wounds
Flamethrowers 40 or less 70%, burned

A man reached by flame is out of the fight with critical burns, and 40% of them are killed outright. A knocked-out bunker is a hex like any other.

For the GM

Under modern fire the question each exchange is who can see whom. Units in the open in close order are cut down. Spread out and gone to ground, they are hard to hit but are pinned half the time. Let the players find a way to move: smoke, a fire plan, a covered approach, or the dark.

Fixed lines

Before dark a machine gun can be laid on a fixed line. In the dark, with no target it can see, it fires blind down the line at an enemy within 1 hex of it, at −15%. The enemy commander, holding, lays its machine guns' lines by day or at dusk on the nearest enemy it knows of in reach, or else ahead toward one (or straight ahead) as far as it can reach and see, shifting such a line once onto an enemy that comes into reach off it.

Armour and mines

On the field map, tanks, infantry fighting vehicles and armoured carriers fight as units, one vehicle to a hex. The unit's men are its crews. They belong to the wars with machine guns or later; the page leaves that to the GM and does not stop him.

Vehicle Crew Move (hexes) Armour Main gun: reach, rounds, hits (close / mid / full) Carries
Tanks 4 12 heavy 1 a vehicle, reach and hits by its fire control (below) —
Infantry fighting vehicles 3 14 light 875 yards (800 m), 2 a vehicle, hits 70/45/20% 7 men
Armoured carriers 3 14 light machine guns only 10 men
Gun tractors and trucks 2 12 soft machine guns only tows 1 gun
Lorries 2 14 soft machine guns only 20 men
Ontos (106 mm recoilless rifles) 3 14 light 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 1 a vehicle, hits 75/50/25% —
  • Moving. Vehicles cross open and high ground at a hex for a hex, and rough ground, slopes and woods for more. They cannot enter marsh, scrub and orchard, buildings, tall buildings, rubble or water, so in a town they keep to the streets.
  • Their machine guns fire as a machine-gun team's, about one gun to a vehicle.
  • Main guns fire each exchange at the nearest enemy in range, in sight and in front, enemy vehicles first, with a clear line of fire. A tank's gun hits and reaches by its fire control, its war's unless the battlefield gives its own:
Fire control Reach Hits a vehicle (first round, at a standing target) Its wars
Optical sight 1,640 yards (1,500 m) 75% to 219 yards (200 m), 50% to 547 yards (500 m), 25% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 5% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m) WWII, Korea
Stadia reticle 1.2 miles (2 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 35% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 4% to 1.2 miles (2 km) Vietnam
Laser rangefinder 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Late 20th century
Thermal fire control 1.9 miles (3 km) 98% to 547 yards (500 m), 94% to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), 75% to 1,640 yards (1,500 m), 55% to 1.2 miles (2 km), 35% to 1.9 miles (3 km) Iraq & Afghanistan
  • Armour. Small arms cannot hurt an armoured vehicle, and men armed only with them do not shoot at one. Trucks and gun tractors are soft-skinned: rifles and machine guns shoot at them too, every shot aimed, and each hit knocks one out at the chance below. No one fights a vehicle hand to hand.

Knocking them out

Rocket teams fire a round for every 4 men each exchange, and missile teams one for every 10. Every round is aimed. A rocket's range, cover and the weather count as for shots at men; a guided missile hits at 85% at any range, less cover and the weather. Fired at men, a rocket is aimed at the hex and bursts there if it hits, striking each man in the hex as a tank's round does; in a building, a tank's round or a rocket bursts in the room and strikes each man there at half. A hit knocks the vehicle out at:

A hit from Heavy armour (tanks) Light armour Soft-skinned (trucks, tractors)
A rocket (RPG, bazooka, recoilless rifle) 15% 50% 80%
A guided missile 60% 90% 95%
A main gun 35% 75% 90%
A rifle or machine-gun bullet — — 5%
  • Where it is hit. A hit into the flank counts ×2, and into the rear ×3, to 100% at most. Which it is depends on where the shooter stands.
  • Composite armour (a battlefield gives it to the M1A1): as heavy armour, but a main gun's round from its front does not knock it out.
  • Short of that, a hit may put the gun out or immobilise the vehicle; shells and bombs bursting in its hex knock it out at their own chance; a vehicle knocked out puts its crew out of the fight. The damage, shell and crew figures are in Knocking out in full.

Anti-tank guns

In the Second World War and Korea, a unit can be anti-tank guns (the British 6-pounder, the American 57 mm, the German Pak 38 and 40, the Soviet 45 mm, the Japanese 47 mm), 5 men to a gun. Each fires 1 round an exchange as a tank's main gun does, out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m); its crews manhandle it, or a tractor tows it; its shield turns small arms from in front. Any gun unit may be emplaced before the battle: hidden and harder to hit, but it cannot move. The crews, towing, rounds, shields and pits are in Anti-tank guns in full.

Minefields

From 1939, the GM can paint minefields before the battle, marked or hidden. A hidden field shows on the map only once something has gone into it. A unit that moves into minefield hexes sets them off before the exchange's shooting. The ground it crossed is reckoned along the cheapest way it could have gone within its move that crosses the fewest minefield hexes its side knows of, so a known field it went round is not set off; a hidden one on its way is.

Minefield Each man going into a hex struck Each vehicle going into a hex struck
Anti-personnel mines 10% —
Anti-tank mines — 30%
Mixed minefield 8% 25%
  • Men. A man struck rolls a wound as one hit by a mine, at 70%. Mine wounds fall mostly on the feet and legs.
  • Vehicles. A vehicle struck is knocked out at 25% (heavy or composite armour), 60% (light) or 80% (soft-skinned). Otherwise a track is blown off and it is immobilised.

  • Sappers. In set-up the GM can mark a foot unit as sappers. On its own side's move, before it moves and out of contact, it can start to lay mines of any kind or to lift them. While it works it neither moves nor fires. Moving, turning, breaking or coming into contact stops the work.

    • Laying takes 3 exchanges. Then the row of hexes just ahead of its front, as wide as its front, is a hidden minefield. Hexes where a unit stands are left clear.
    • Lifting takes 2 exchanges. Then the minefield hexes in that row that its side knows of are lifted: a lane.
    • The enemy commander sets its own sappers to work (see the enemy commander).
    • A side knows the mines its own sappers laid: its commander steers round them, and they do not strike its own men.

Riders

Infantry fighting vehicles, carriers and lorries carry men, and tanks carry 6 men on each hull. A foot unit beside them can mount if all its men fit and neither unit is in contact. Riders move with the vehicles. Men in an infantry fighting vehicle shoot through its ports (25% of them) and men on a tank's hull shoot from it (50%), at their own weapon's target; otherwise riders do not fight, shoot or check morale until they dismount beside them. When a carrier is knocked out, each of its riders is struck at 30%, as by shellfire. Lorries are soft-skinned: a rifle or machine-gun hit that does not knock one out strikes a man aboard. Men riding on a tank's hull are in the open: small arms shoot at the tanks for them, and each hit strikes a rider; shells bursting near the tanks strike them as men in the open.

Air and night devices

For aircraft, troops landed by air, and the devices that see in the dark: from the Second World War for aircraft, from Vietnam for helicopters and night vision (the page leaves the dates to the GM).

Night vision

  • Night vision. From the 1960s, units can carry devices that see further in the dark. Vehicles carry their war's unless another is chosen: infrared searchlights in Vietnam, thermal sights from the 1980s on. No device sees past the weather's own limit, a sandstorm's included.
  • Infrared beams. A vehicle that fires in the dark by its infrared searchlight lights its target with a beam that enemy infrared sets, Starlight scopes and goggles pick up: through the next exchange, those enemies can aim at the hexes it fired from out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m). A thermal sight does not see the beam.
  • Washed out. A unit standing in a flare's or illumination round's light cannot use a Starlight scope, goggles or infrared set (its men see the dark beyond with their own eyes), and an infrared searchlight there shows no beam. Thermal sights are not washed out.
Device Sees to Aims at worst Through smoke
Starlight scope (1960s-70s) 219 yards (200 m) −15% —
Night-vision goggles (1990s on) 328 yards (300 m) −5% —
Thermal sight (tanks from the 1980s, teams from the 2000s) 656 yards (600 m) as by day yes
Infrared searchlight and sights (tanks, 1950s-70s) 175 yards (160 m) −20% —

Aircraft

Fighter-bombers and helicopter gunships are called like batteries; each "tube" is an aircraft. Fire can be called only where one of the side's units can see it fall.

Aircraft Comes An aircraft an exchange In all Scatter Struck % at 0, 1, 2 … hexes By night
Fighter-bombers (bombs, napalm) 2 exchanges after the call 2 bombs 4 3 hexes 45, 25, 12, 5, 2 no
Helicopter gunships (rockets, guns) at once 4 rocket and gun passes 24 1 hex 20, 6 yes
  • Weather. Aircraft do not fly in fog, storm, heavy snow, blizzard, sandstorm, and fighter-bombers do not fly at night. A mission called then waits until the weather clears.

  • Strafing and napalm. An air attack can be a strafing run or (fighter-bombers, from 1944) a napalm strip, flown along a line the GM chooses. Each pass covers 5 hexes strafing or 3 with napalm.

    • Strafing strikes each man there at 12%, less cover and for going to ground.
    • Napalm strikes at 45% and nothing protects. It puts a man down with critical burns, and kills 35% outright.
    • Marking the target. Smoke laid on the aimed hex before the aircraft arrive halves their scatter, as an air controller does.

    • Ground fire. After each attack run, every aircraft that attacked can be hit.

    • Small arms within 328 yards (300 m) of the aim: 0.5% for each machine gun served there, 1% for each unit with rockets, and 0.2% for every 100 men with other firearms, at most 12% in all.

    • Anti-aircraft guns within 1,094 yards (1,000 m) add 3% for each gun served.

    Gunships fly low and slow, so they count it ×2. The whole is at most 35%. Of the aircraft hit, 40% are brought down; the rest are damaged and turn for home.

  • Air controllers. A unit can be given a forward air controller. When he can see the aim, the attack scatters half as far. Without one, aircraft will not attack within 109 yards (100 m) of their own men; the mission waits until it can.

Landing by air

From Vietnam on (the page leaves the date to the GM), units can come in by helicopter to a landing zone. Each side has so many helicopters: by default X-Ray's 16 Hueys of 5 men each, back for the next load 30 exchanges after they land. At the end of each exchange the free ones fly the lifts in the order called, at most 8 at a zone. The men land on the zone or the nearest spot within 4 hexes, and can move the next exchange.

  • Waved off. No one lands while an enemy unit stands within 2 hexes of the zone.
  • Turned back. Once the men of a unit already down have broken, the rest of its lift turns back.
  • A hot zone. If any enemy unit could shoot at the zone, each man landing is struck at 10% and wounded as by shellfire, and each helicopter is hit at 10%: 20% of those come down on the zone as a wreck, the rest go home damaged. Either way it is lost for the battle.
  • Supplies and extraction. A helicopter can set a supply dump down on a zone, and the helicopters can lift a unit out from near a zone (out of contact; it does not move while it boards). Its men flown out are safe.
  • A downed helicopter gives the men in its hex cover and is slow ground to cross.

How the pages work

The main chapters say what each rule means for play. This appendix holds the procedures the pages compute for you, in full, so that the game can still be played on paper and checked by hand. Each section belongs to the rule it is linked from.

An exchange in full

For An exchange.

  1. Who strikes. In melee, the front rank of each hex touching the enemy, and one more rank for each hex of the weapon's reach past the first (spears and bills strike from two ranks, the pike from three). With missiles, the men who have the target in range.
  2. How many blows tell. Most of a minute in a press is shoving and watching for an opening: about one striking man in 11 makes a real attempt each exchange. A longbowman looses 8 arrows a minute, and about one shot in 30 is aimed at a man rather than loosed at the mass.
  3. Each attempt is one attack, at the unit's quality, exactly as in the fight: +20 from the flank and +30 from the rear (and no parry from either), +20 and twice as many attempts for a mounted charge in its first exchange, −10 for a shaken unit, +20 for pikes in close order against horse to their front; range, weather and cover come off missiles. A tired unit loses its fatigue level's penalty off its attack and its parry.
  4. The wound is rolled as for one man. A light wound or a graze: he fights on. Serious or critical: a stop check, and failing it puts him down. A wound that kills within rounds kills. A module can change who goes down: Modern fire puts more men down.
  5. Morale, below; then the next exchange.

Fatigue. A unit tires as a character does. Each exchange it fights hand to hand counts one toil, and so does each hex it goes in deep mud or snow. After 12 toil in heavy armour, 20 in medium, or 30 in light, it is a fatigue step worse, to Exhausted at most, and stays so for the battle. Shooting costs none, and vehicles don't tire.

Ammunition in full

For Ammunition.

A unit that shoots carries only so much. Its load is counted in exchanges of fire: the rounds, arrows or bolts a man carries (a machine gun's belts, for a gun), over the rate it fires at, times 30% (men do not fire every round they could). Longbowmen have about 20 exchanges of shooting, riflemen of 1914-53 about 40, a machine gun about 22. Vehicles and guns count their own rounds.

  • Running low. Each exchange it shoots uses one. At 25% of a full load or less it shoots at half rate; with none it cannot shoot at all, still fights hand to hand, and has -10 on morale.
  • Resupply. An exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing, within 5 hexes of a supply source: its side's map edge (behind the way most of its men face), a lorry or armoured carrier of its side, or a supply dump. The GM places dumps before the battle (a battlefield may come with its own, as the stores in RIR 119's dugouts at Beaumont-Hamel); from the Second World War on, an air drop called on a side's move lands as a dump at the end of the exchange, a little off the mark, and from Vietnam on a helicopter can set one down on a landing zone (Landing by air).
  • The enemy commander resupplies a unit that is out, or low with no enemy in its range, when a source is in reach. Attacking, a unit out of ammunition with none in reach falls back toward its edge; holding, it stays and fights hand to hand.

The enemy commander

For The enemy commander.

The GM can hand one side to a scripted enemy commander, attacking or holding. At the start of that side's move it orders each unit. It knows only the enemies its units can see (or saw in the last 3 exchanges, where they were then; what a unit sees from where it has just moved, the units ordered after it know); green units go for the nearest, better ones for an enemy that is hurt, shaken or dangerous to them. It closes, takes cover, shoots from range or charges with the odds its quality wants (counting the steady friends touching it, who go in with it), and green units sometimes hesitate. With no enemy in sight, a unit holds; attacking with no objective, it goes forward along its facing to find one. A unit with no room to move facing its goal (or a turn too dear) moves facing as near its goal as it can. A unit on the ground turns to face its target where it lies, and stays down.

  • Storming works. Attacking infantry close on an enemy behind works (a parapet, trench or bank), dug in, or in buildings or rubble, as the module for their weapons says: with muskets, rifle-muskets and breech-loaders, Black-powder guns; with modern rifles and sub-machine guns, Modern infantry. Archers, flintlock riflemen and machine guns fight by fire.

  • Routes. A battlefield can send a unit on a route round a flank, as its account tells: the commander moves it from waypoint to waypoint, turning aside only for an enemy in contact or across its way, then orders it as any other.

  • Orders from the accounts. On the battlefields, units that the sources say held their ground fight where they stand rather than fall back, and units the sources say withdrew on orders fall back at the minute the accounts give, to a place or off the field.
  • Narrowing. Attacking, a formed unit that the ground keeps from closing on its target closes in its front, a quarter at a time and deeper, until it can move nearer, but never to less than half the front it started with.
  • Pursuit. Its horse ride down a broken enemy within a charge when no standing enemy is as near, and its foot go after one within their move that is nearer than any standing enemy. Veterans rally back to the fight after a couple of moves if the enemy still stands near.
  • Shooters give way. Attacking, archers, crossbowmen and skirmishers in open order step aside when they stand in the way of their own formed men behind them, and the formed men go on.
  • In range means the weapon reaches, the light lets it see, and nothing blocks the line from where it would stand.
  • Reserve. Regulars and veterans hold back their rearmost units (not one on a route, nor tanks and other vehicles with a main gun), and commit one when a unit of theirs breaks or the enemy comes close; veterans also commit to exploit an enemy rout. Attacking, they also commit one when the attack has stalled: five moves without putting down any real share of the enemy or getting nearer. A unit committed because one broke goes to plug the gap where it stood. The GM can mark reserves instead.
  • Objective. The GM can mark a hex as its objective. Attacking, its units advance on it when they have nothing better to do and hold it once there (within 1 hex), but go on attacking while their target is on it too; holding, units more than 3 hexes from it fall back to it. Enemies near it make better targets. The log says who holds it after each exchange. Most battlefields mark the place their battle was fought for, a hill, a bridge, an outpost, as theirs, taking in the whole position (a ring of trenches counts as the hill). The GM can also mark a second objective. Attacking, once it holds the first, the units on it stay and the rest go on to the second (and back to the first if the enemy retakes it); holding, once the enemy holds the first, its units fall back to the second.
  • Guns. It turns its guns to face the enemy. Attacking, guns with no enemy in reach go forward and stop in reach, but no nearer than 2 hexes; holding, they stay where they stand. Attacking or holding, guns an enemy could reach at a charge, with no steady friend on the line between, pull back as far as they can from it.
  • Modules. What it does with batteries, shellfire, vehicles, mines and aircraft is in the modules that bring them: Black-powder guns, Modern fire, Armour and mines and Air and night devices.

Undo its orders puts the move back for the GM to make by hand.

Both sides. Each side has its own choice: moved by the GM, or the commander attacking or holding. With the commander on both sides the GM only watches: Next steps a move at a time, and Run plays on until the GM presses Stop or the run ends itself. It ends when a side has no unit left standing and none still to come, when an attacking side has taken the objective and held it 5 exchanges running with no enemy standing within 109 yards (100 m) of it and none still to come (but not before the battlefield's last phase has begun), or after 60 exchanges (on a battlefield with phases, 30 past the last phase's start, if later, but never more than 1200); then the battle ends, as with End the battle. On a battlefield the side its objective names attacks and the other holds, or the armies fight as the battlefield says they did (the choice marked as fought); on open ground both attack. The GM can take either side back at any time.

The narrative. Under the map, the page tells the battle's turning points as they happen: a phase beginning (and who comes on), units breaking or fleeing, a reserve committed, the objective taken or lost, and the end with each side's losses. With an API key of the player's own (a free one serves), or a model run on the player's own computer, a language model retells each one in a short passage of at most 70 words, in a voice for the war (a chronicle, a dispatch, a war diary or a situation report), or one the GM picks for the battle (any of those, a soldier's account or a plain summary). It is told to use only the facts the game gives it and to write original prose; the plain line stays under each passage. The rules never depend on it.

With Black-powder guns

With this module, the enemy commander also moves its batteries: attacking, a battery with no enemy in reach limbers, moves, and unlimbers once an enemy is in reach; holding, it unlimbers where it stands; to pull back from a charge it limbers first.

With Modern fire

With this module, the enemy commander also:

  • Digging in. Its foot units with modern weapons dig in where they stand when it is safe (not under fire, no enemy it knows of in their range): at the objective, holding with no objective, and in reserve while they wait.
  • Shellfire. It calls its off-map batteries on what it sees, closer to its own men first. Attacking, one battery lays a creeping barrage ahead of a unit closing on the enemy, and first has one battery smoke an enemy that is shooting at men who cannot reply (not in the dark, or in a gale). Its batteries under counter-battery fire displace (a placed one moves its place 30 hexes along its map edge, away from the battery firing). In the dark it first has one battery fire illumination over the enemy it has lost sight of nearest its men, where it was last seen. Then one battery fires counter-battery on a located enemy battery it can reach: the one with the best counter % on the one with the most guns still served.

With Armour and mines

With this module, the enemy commander also:

  • Tanks. A unit with a main gun counts the target in range where the gun reaches and it can see; a vehicle with one prefers a spot where the target can neither reach it nor see it. Any shooter counts a target in range only where the weather and light let it see that far. Attacking, a vehicle unit leaves its immobilised vehicles behind and goes on with the rest.
  • Minefields. It steers round minefields it knows of. Its sappers, attacking, lift a lane through known enemy mines in the row ahead when those mines lie on the way to their target or the objective, closing up to the belt first and working through it row by row. Holding, or at the objective, with no enemy it knows of within 8 hexes, they lay mines in the row ahead: mixed if the enemy it knows of has vehicles, otherwise anti-personnel.
  • Towing and carriers. Attacking, its anti-tank guns with no enemy in reach hook up to an empty tractor beside them (an empty tractor drives over to fetch them), are towed, and are unhooked in reach; holding, they unhook where they stand, and to pull back they hook up. Attacking, its foot units get aboard empty carriers beside them while no known enemy is in reach, and get down once one is (or at the objective).

For the GM

Armour is a problem the infantry must solve, not a fight it can win with rifles. Give the side without tanks rockets, anti-tank guns, mines, ground the tanks cannot cross, or the dark.

With Air and night devices

With this module, the enemy commander also:

  • Aircraft. It calls its aircraft (when they can fly; a strafing run or napalm strip along a wide enemy front) on what it sees, first what its forward air controllers see, and closer to its own men there. A controller with nothing to do and no target in its sight moves up to where it sees one (attacking only), up to 3 moves away, a move at a time, preferring a spot out of the enemy's reach; not while it has a fight of its own (an enemy touching it or in its own reach, pinned, or men lost the exchange before).

Batteries in full

For Guns of the black-powder wars.

A battery is a unit in battery order, 20 men to a hex. Its men are the crews, 10 to a gun, so as crews fall fewer guns are served.

  • Its fire. Each served gun fires a round an exchange at the nearest enemy in front of it, in sight and with a clear line of fire, out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m) (1,750 yards (1,600 m) for rifled guns). The GM can name another target, split the guns into sections, or choose the shot.
  • Canister. Within 328 yards (300 m) the guns fire canister: 8 chances a round, each likely to hit at short range and less so beyond.
  • Round shot. Beyond that range the guns fire round shot. A ball that strikes a unit ploughs through its ranks, and each man in its path is hit at 40%, so a deep column suffers far more than a line. On firm ground the ball bounds on, and it can strike another unit up to 328 yards (300 m) beyond.
  • Shell. Howitzers fire shell over anything in the way. Its fuse may burst it early, in the air over the men, on the ground, or not at all. Gunners who have found the range cut their fuses better.
  • Wounds. Every man struck by a gun rolls a wound at 80%, with no parry.
  • Rounds. Each gun carries 50 rounds into action. Resupply takes an exchange.
  • Limbering. Changing between limbered and unlimbered takes an exchange. Unlimbered, the guns can only be pushed 2 hexes.
  • Losing the guns. A battery that breaks loses its guns for good.
  • Canister at the charge. Charged in front, a battery gives the first charger one round of canister at point-blank range before the melee.

Knocking out in full

For Knocking them out.

  • Morale. A vehicle unit's morale checks count whole vehicles lost, not crewmen hit in vehicles still fighting.

  • Damage short of that. A hit that does not knock the vehicle out strikes the turret at 35%, else the hull.

    • On the turret it puts the main gun out at 40%, and immobilises the vehicle at only 5%.
    • On the hull it immobilises the vehicle at 35%, and puts the gun out at 5%.

    Immobilised vehicles can still turn. Their crews can abandon them and leave the fight unhurt.

  • Shells and bombs bursting in a vehicle's hex knock it out at the kind's own chance: a heavy howitzer's 2%, a fighter-bomber's 15%. Light armour is 3 times as likely to go, soft-skinned vehicles 6 times.

  • Knocked out. Its crew are out of the fight. Each is struck at 50% and wounded as by shellfire; the rest bail out.

Anti-tank guns in full

For Anti-tank guns.

In the Second World War and Korea, a unit can be anti-tank guns: towed guns such as the British 6-pounder, the American 57 mm, the German Pak 38 and 40, the Soviet and North Korean 45 mm and the Japanese 47 mm.

  • Crews. Each gun has 5 men. A gun fires while one of its crew is up, and its crews manhandle it 2 hexes.
  • Fire. Each gun fires 1 round an exchange, as a tank's main gun does. Out to 1,094 yards (1,000 m), it hits a vehicle at 70/45/20% (close, mid and full range), and the hit then knocks the vehicle out as a main gun's would. At men, its high explosive bursts as a tank's round does.
  • Towing. Gun tractors and trucks tow a gun each, the crews riding. Hooked up beside them, the guns move with the tractors and do not fire; unhooked, they fire from the next exchange.
  • Rounds. Each gun brings 40 rounds. A gun out of them is resupplied as a battery is: an exchange out of contact, neither moving nor firing.
  • Shields. Anti-tank and anti-aircraft guns have shields: small arms fired at them from in front lose 30%. Shields do nothing against shells or fire from the flank or rear. Some machine guns had shields too (a Maxim on a wheeled mount, say), though most did not: in set-up the GM can mark a machine-gun unit shielded, and it gets the same cover.
  • Vulnerable. Otherwise its crews are men: rifles, machine guns and shells strike them, and hand to hand they fight with bayonets.
  • Emplaced. Before the battle the GM can dig in any gun unit (anti-tank guns, anti-aircraft guns, machine guns or a battery). While it stands it counts as gone to ground, −15% and hidden, but it cannot move all battle, though it can turn. A unit that breaks leaves its pits.
  • The enemy commander tows its anti-tank guns forward and unhooks them in reach (see the enemy commander).

The campaign in full

These rules matter in a long campaign, or when their case comes up in play. The main chapters say each in brief and link here.

Tongues in full

For Tongues.

Related tongues. A tongue he lacks he knows at a share of a related one he has (half of German from Low German, three quarters of English from Scots). Pidgins rise no higher than 35 (Bamboo English in Korea, GI Vietnamese), the Plains sign language no higher than 75, and a learned tongue no higher than 85.

Phrase books. From the Crimea on, armies issued phrase books: across tongues, a yes or no, a number or a pointed direction is then Easy at no worse than 25.

Passing as a native. His figure against the listener's Watch (both roll): Ordinary in his own tongue, Hard fluent without the idiom (76+), Very hard a good speaker (51-75), and below that he cannot pass. In 1944 Skorzeny found ten men with perfect English and idiom for Operation Greif, thirty or forty good speakers, and over a hundred moderate ones; those caught in American uniform were shot.

Taken and escaping. A man who asks for quarter in his captors' tongue is a little safer (the capture roll is 10 better: a surrender had to be accepted to protect him). Escaping, his Fieldcraft to get home is +10 if he converses in their tongue and +20 if it is his own.

On the travel map the people where a force stands speak a tongue, or in mixed country several: the nearest town, village or landmark within 6 miles (10 km) decides (its own, if it names them), and everywhere else has the map's. A force with no named man who gets by in any of them forages Hard, its talk is in the best of them he has, and a month among them ticks their main tongue. The map shows a place's tongues when you point at it.

Learning. A tongue used well is ticked and rolls to rise at End of season like a skill (one at 0 always rises). A month among its speakers on the travel map, or a season held prisoner, ticks it; so does a week with a language master, a teammate who speaks it well, or (from 1943) an army course. The army's courses took three months for the better students to order a meal or rent a room; the Foreign Legion's recruits answered in French within ten days.

Interpreters. The team may hire an interpreter for a season: a man of the other army who speaks the team's tongue and his own at 50 to 85 (rolled). He costs 1 Day a day (0.4 for the modern wars, where Iraqi interpreters began at $600 a month in 2005). A man who talks through him uses the interpreter's figure in that tongue, not his own. Of those hired 28% are unreliable (a whistleblower said 28% of one firm's Afghan hires failed the language standard): his roll of 90 or more is a dangerous error. Each End of season he may be killed (0.5%, 1% in the modern wars: in Iraq some fifteen times a US soldier's rate), and his season is up. On the travel map, where the people speak his tongue and the team's named men march with the force, he forages and talks for it: the force does not forage Hard for want of the tongue, and its billeting and talk go through him at his figure.

Who speaks what, by army (the shares are estimates, not muster counts):

Each army's tongues: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Age and wear in full

For Age and wear.

Enlisting. A man enlists at his era's starting age, raised to his army's legal least (15 to 60 under the Statute of Winchester; 17 to 25 for Victorian recruits; 18 to 37 in the American draft of 1942). Then d100: a few are boys under age (about a tenth of the Union army was under 18), enlisted at up to 3 years below the least, and a few older recruits, from 38 up to 6 years past the most (over it, he lied). A man under or over age is found out at 10% each End of season and sent home, until he is of age (a boy) or has served out his first term (an older man). Most characters are made after their terms, so a boy's lie matters only in the eras of one-year terms. A recruit who enlisted at 38 or more takes 2 times the Wear for his service: Union men enlisting at about 39 had 1.8 times the odds of dying of disease of men of 20 in their first year, and 2.4 after.

A man ages with his terms. For every 4 years of his life past the start of his service (at the making of a character, the years of his terms; in play, each term served) he rolls his age band's decline, taken from his characteristics as a lasting hurt is (his skills that rest on them fall with them), and, from 20, gains a step of maturity: +1 Presence and +1 Nerve until 40, +1 Wits until 45 (at most +5 each). Each promotion adds +2 Presence, to +6 in all (a design estimate: a man who leads grows into it). Endurance goes first, then Agility, then Strength; Wits slows from 50:

Age (middle of the 4 years) Strength Agility Endurance Wits
30–39 — −d3 −d2 —
40–49 −d3 −d4 −d4 —
50–59 −d4 −d6 −d6 −d2
60 and over −d6 −2d4 −2d4 −d2

Wear. Service wears a man: +1 Wear for each 4 years, and +1 for each hard season (a month of hard nights on the travel map, hungry, sick or wounded, or colder and wetter than his shelter; or the GM's word for a siege, a famine or a tropical station). Each 4 Wear makes him 2 years older for his decline, and from 6 Wear his Endurance rolls twice and takes the worse.

Worn out. For each term he serves from 35, or with 8 Wear or more, he rolls d100: at or under 3 × Wear + 2 × (his age − 35) − (Endurance − 50) ÷ 2, he is worn out (a 1-year term rolls a quarter of that). From 40, Endurance under 30, or Strength, Agility or Endurance under 25, wears him out at once. The GM may send him home (with a pension where his army gave one) or keep him on. British soldiers discharged "worn out" were mostly 41 to 44, after 21 to 25 years.

Training in full

For Training.

Training. A skill can also be ticked by a week's teaching: from a master for hire where the team is (a riding master, a master of defence, a schoolmaster, a surgeon, a craftsman; his skill counts as 60, and he charges a fee by the week), or from a teammate at least 20 better (who gives up the week too). The teacher rolls his skill; a success ticks the pupil's skill, a failure wastes the week. The pupil pays the fee and his keep; a teammate who teaches loses the week from his next job term. An army drills its men: a week in which a force its army feeds spent four days or more not marching, the best Command with it (or the army's own sergeants, 50) rolls, and on a success each named man's weapon skill is ticked. Riding lessons in London in 1879 cost about six days of a private's pay each; the other fees are estimates.

Courses. Some training takes him away for weeks or a year, for set gains: a year as an apprentice or in a knight's household, two weeks at a Civil War camp of instruction, eighteen months at Sandhurst, four and a half at a 1916 officer cadet battalion, seventeen weeks at an American Officer Candidate School (22 in Korea, 23 in Vietnam, 12 today), Ranger School, the Special Forces course. An army's course counts as service, and an officer's course makes him eligible for its rank at the next vacancy, whatever his rank and years:

Training courses: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Strain in full

For Strain.

A light day in the line, a day in the line, a fight or an extreme day is changed by how he stands with his comrades, summed:

Strain
A trusted leader -25%
Comrades of long standing -25%
A replacement among strangers +25%
On the move (an advance or a withdrawal) -50%

40% of every point also goes into his Toll, which only going home lowers. Each time Strain and Toll together pass 10, 20, 30 and on, he rolls d100: at or under his Nerve + 115 − that total, he holds; a man who has broken down before rolls 10 less, and a roll of 99 or more always fails. If he fails, he rolls d10, adding 1 for each 10 he failed by: 1-4 shaken (−10 to attack and Nerve until a day's rest), 5-7 strained (−20 until treated), 8-9 broken down (out of the fight until treated), 10 or more severely (out, and to be sent back). Each era has its own words for these: nostalgia in the Napoleonic and Civil wars, shell shock in 1914-18, combat exhaustion in 1944.

A day out of the line, camped, takes 3.5 Strain off. A man who breaks down is treated where he is, near the front or in the rear; the nearer and the sooner, the likelier he goes back to duty, and treatment takes Strain off him (sent home, all of it, and half his Toll):

Where Days Strain off Back to duty: shaken strained broken down severely
With his unit (comrades, a sergeant, a priest) 2 10 60% 60% 30% 10%
A forward exhaustion centre (from 1916) 3 20 70% 65% 60% 30%
A hospital in the rear 14 30 50% 40% 30% 20%
Sent home 60 all 30% 20% 13% 10%
Furlough home (before 1914) 30 all 60% 50% 40% 30%

Except treatment with his unit, he is away from the force for those days: the travel map counts them off, and he comes back to it when they are done. If the team's leader is killed, each of his men takes the Strain of it (3), twice that if he was a trusted leader (Command 60 or more): a design estimate, since no study measured it.

Korea, Vietnam and the later wars rotated men home at the end of a tour: Strain gone, the Toll cut to a quarter. For the Plains nations, a homecoming that welcomes and honours a man halves it. A man who ends a campaign with his Toll at or above his Nerve, or who broke down, may carry a lasting effect: the GM notes it as part of who he is (sleeping badly, starting at noises, drinking, grief), never as a penalty.

On the road in full

For On the road.

An army loses men without a battle. Each night every fit man takes his era's chance of deserting, of falling out and being lost to the force, and of being injured (a fall, a kick, an accident: he joins the sick and wounded), and every man of a mounted force or a wagon train of losing his horse. The chances depend on what the force did that day: in camp they are small (Valley Forge lost 3 men in 10,000 a day to desertion); on the march larger; and withdrawing far larger (the retreat to Corunna lost 1 in 100 a day, the British retreat from Mons nearly 2). A big force simply loses more men. Then there is a chance of an incident: a d100 on the era's table (foragers set on by peasants, a bridge down, a convoy ambushed, a mine in the road, a checkpoint), some for small parties or wagons only, some costing men or a step of fatigue, each with a hook for the GM. The rates come from the records where they exist and are estimates where they do not; the incidents are estimates. At the GM's choice, named characters take the injury chance too.

A force short of food deserts about fifteen times as fast (the starving camp at Nuremberg in 1632) and straggles five times; one whose pay is in arrears deserts three times as fast. The larger applies, not both. A mounted force keeps its count of horses: lost horses, and the horses its deserters ride off on, come off it, and under half a horse a man it marches at foot pace. A wagon train short of teams slows to three quarters, and under half its teams to half. The GM adds remounts when the force finds them.

Boots and clothing in full

For Boots and clothing.

Each named man's boots wear with every day he marches, faster on wet or muddy ground, and his clothing and blankets with every day, twice as fast on a hard night. Lives in days:

How long boots and clothing last: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Worn boots raise his chance of blistered feet (half again; worn out, three times); worn clothing makes his nights a step colder and wetter (worn out, two), for his recovery and for frostbite. On a day his force does not march, its best Craft mends the most worn boots or clothing among its named men (Mend kit: a success takes off half a life's wear, a fumble ruins them). He may buy new from the price list (boots, shoes, a coat, a blanket), and a force its army feeds is issued new at its depot. In October 1862 the 48th North Carolina returned 51 of its 619 men barefoot and 194 more nearly so; at Valley Forge 2,898 men were unfit for duty, "barefoot and otherwise naked".

Supplies in full

For Supplies.

A force carries what it needs between fights: ammunition (a share of its full loads), rations (days a man carries), water (litres a man) and medical stores:

Rations and water carried: each period's figures are in its book: The Medieval Wars, The Black-Powder Wars, The World Wars, Korea and Vietnam, The Late Wars.

Rations. A day its army does not feed it, and it has not foraged or hunted its food, it eats a day's rations; with none left it goes hungry (desertion and straggling run higher, and its named men have a hard night). A Union quartermaster reckoned that of eight days issued, hardly five could be counted on. Water. By a river, lake, ford, marsh, bridge, village or town, or in rain, it fills up; elsewhere each man needs 2 L on a cool day, 3 L on a warm one, 5 L in heat and 8 L in great heat; short of it, the force is thirsty: a step more fatigue and a hard night. Medical stores serve 10 wounded or sick for each hundred men; each new wounded man draws one and each sick man a seventh a day; with none left its sick and wounded are cared for a step worse in camp. Ammunition goes into a battle on the field map as its share of a load, and what is left comes back.

It refills everything at its army's depot (where it started on the map, or a place marked a depot of its side, flagged ⚑ on the map: Harfleur and Calais for Henry V, Balaklava and Kamiesh before Sevastopol, Hagaru-ri and Koto-ri at Chosin), draws from its baggage train in the same hex (the train carries 10 days' rations, 2 loads of ammunition and 2 fills of medical stores for 1,000 men, and a larger force takes more of it), and where its army does not feed it its named men may buy a day's rations for every man in a village or town at their army's keep.

Sickness in full

For Sickness.

Before antibiotics, disease emptied armies faster than battle. Once a week every well man may catch what the camp breeds, at a chance set by its hygiene (a bivouac is poor, quarters good, other camps fair), by staying four weeks or more in one place, by the ground (marsh, a town) and by the week's weather:

Disease Caught from Shows after Deaths per case (records)
Bloody flux Dirty water or food, latrines too near the water 1–3 days 2.6%
Camp fever (typhus) Lice in crowded, unwashed camps 7–14 days 40%
Typhoid Dirty water or food, often from a carrier in camp 7–21 days 36%
Ague (malaria) Mosquitoes in marshes and low wetlands 7–28 days 0.8%
Plague Flea bites; worst in sieges and towns full of rats 2–6 days 45%

A case climbs to its peak after it shows, then gets better or worse each night on the track of Recovery, with rest, a camp and shelter helping, and marching, cold wet nights and filth hurting. Survivors of typhus and plague cannot catch it again; ague comes back in marsh country.

  • What it costs. Men at serious or worse cannot dig, fight or march on their own; at grave or worse they are carried on litters. A force carrying litters marches at 90%, or 50% with fewer than 2 fit men a litter.
  • Scurvy. After 6 weeks without fresh food (fruit, greens, fresh meat, onions), each week every well man may fall ill: 10% the first week, 10 more each week after, against his Endurance. Fresh food heals it 2 steps a week. A scurvied man's old wounds open again.
  • Frostbite. On a night of 5 °F (-15 °C) or colder, men without enough shelter may be frostbitten, a sickness on the same track.
